title: Asking Questions
description: The full set of question words — what, who, why, how, which, how many — and the questions every Yemeni will ask you in the first five minutes: where from, married, children, how old. With the polite ways to answer and to deflect.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — question and answer pairs heard whole before the question words are isolated; the learner answers before they ask.
unlock_condition: ≥10/14 on the question-word match and a recorded exchange answering the four small-talk questions
can_do: Ask what, who, why, how, which, how many, when and where
Answer the small-talk questions everyone asks

grammar.title: Question words: in front, or where the answer would go
grammar.explanation: Yemeni question words can stand at the front of the sentence, as in English, or stay exactly where the answer will sit: أنت من وين؟ literally 'you from where?'. Both are natural; the end position is warmer and more conversational. The Sanaa word for 'who' is من, said man — which looks like 'from' on the page, so this app teaches the clearer مين and you recognise both. For 'why', ليش is what you will say; older Sanaa speakers also have للمه.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions are just a rising voice
grammar.explanation: There is no word for turning a statement into a yes/no question. Say the statement and let your voice rise at the end: أنت متزوج؟ 'You're married?'. The Sanaa 'yes' is إي — short and very common — and 'no' is لا. To offer two choices use ولا: شاهي ولا قهوة؟

examples.english: Do you have kids? — Yes, three
Do you want tea or coffee?

culture.title: The friendly interrogation
culture.note: Within minutes of meeting you, a Yemeni will ask where you are from, whether you are married, how many children you have, what you do and — quite possibly — what you earn. None of it is rude; it is how a stranger is placed. Answer briefly and ask the same back: it is a conversation, not a form. If you are unmarried, 'not yet, God willing' is the expected reply, and a smile plus إن شاء الله deflects almost anything.

phrases.arabic: متزوج؟ — عاد لا، إن شاء الله
phrases.transliteration: mitzawwij? — ʿaad laa, in shaa allaah

phrases.english: What do you do? — I study Arabic here
And you, where are you from?

culture.title: Say yes the Sanaa way: إي
culture.note: The everyday 'yes' in Sanaa is إي, a short open sound — you will hear it hundreds of times a day, on its own or as إي والله. ايوه and نعم are understood but sound imported or formal. Say إي and people relax.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni 'what', from Sanaa to Aden. One syllable: aysh. Older Sanaa keeps classical ما in a few fixed questions (ما اسمك؟); شو and وش are heard from Gulf-facing speakers. Never ماذا.
vocabulary.image_scene: A large question mark over an open hand pointing at an unlabelled box.

example.english: What do you want to drink?

vocabulary.video_hint: Any 'what' question in a skit or interview; ايش is usually the first word.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa's own 'who' is من (man), identical on the page to 'from' — so the app teaches مين, which every Yemeni uses too and nobody mishears. 'Who's this?' is مين ذا؟
vocabulary.image_scene: A silhouette of a person with a question mark for a face.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone pointing at a person in a photo or doorway: 'who's that?'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The one to say. The Sanaa oldies' للمه (lilmah) is worth recognising; ليه is Taizz and Egyptian media. Never لماذا.
vocabulary.image_scene: A child with arms spread wide, asking, in front of a closed shop.
vocabulary.video_hint: Complaints and arguments in comedy skits: 'why didn't you…?'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: You met it inside كيف حالك; alone it asks how something is done or what it is like. شلون exists in Yemen but كيف is the default.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person shrugging with palms up beside a map route.

example.english: How do you get to work?

vocabulary.video_hint: 'How do you…?' questions in cooking or how-to videos.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Pronounced ayy with a doubled y, straight before the noun: أي واحد؟ 'which one?'. أيهم is 'which of them'.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three glasses of tea in a row, a finger hovering over them.
vocabulary.video_hint: A choice being offered: 'which one?', 'which colour?'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Followed by a singular noun, not a plural: كم جاهل؟ 'how many children?'. For a price it becomes بكم (with بـ). Also asks age and time: كم عمرك؟ الساعة كم؟
vocabulary.image_scene: A row of children of different heights with a question mark above them.

example.english: How many children do you have?

vocabulary.video_hint: Counting questions: 'how many people', 'how many years'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Question number two in any first conversation. Feminine متزوجة. The Sanaa word معرّس is also common for a man who has married.
vocabulary.image_scene: A couple's two hands with gold rings, henna on the bride's.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews asking about marriage; wedding-season vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni word for children: one جاهل, many جهّال — from a root meaning 'not yet knowing'. عيال and أولاد are heard too. Doubled ه.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three small children playing football in a dusty Sanaa alley.
vocabulary.video_hint: Family vlogs; the question 'do you have kids?' and its answer.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'How old are you?' is literally 'how much is your age?': كم عمرك؟ (to a woman كم عمرش؟). Answer with عمري + number + سنة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A birthday cake with numeral candles reading 30.

example.english: How old are you? — I'm thirty

vocabulary.video_hint: Kids' Q&A and interviews where age is asked.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The surprised 'really?', said with a rise. صح alone works too. والله؟ is the stronger version; use it sparingly.
vocabulary.image_scene: A listener's face with raised eyebrows and a hand to the chest.
vocabulary.video_hint: Surprised reactions in conversation; often the whole reply.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The filler that buys thinking time and the connector that rephrases. Yemenis use it constantly; so can you, and it hides every pause.
vocabulary.image_scene: A speaker mid-sentence, one hand circling as they search for the word.

example.arabic: أنا يعني مش من هنا، أنا من تعز
example.transliteration: ana yaʿni mish min hina, ana min taʿizz
example.english: I mean, I'm not from here, I'm from Taizz

vocabulary.video_hint: Almost every unscripted clip; listen for it as a pause-filler.

vocabulary.teaching_note: طبعاً keeps its -an ending. 'Of course' alone is طبعاً or أكيد; add لا for the firm denial. Said lightly it is a joke, said flat it closes the subject.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person laughing and waving a hand 'no'.

example.arabic: أنت متزوج؟ — طبعاً لا، عادني صغير
example.transliteration: ant mitzawwij? — ṭabʿan laa, ʿaadni ṣaghiir
example.english: Married? — Of course not, I'm still young

vocabulary.video_hint: Denials in skits: a laugh and 'of course not'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Question number one. Sanaa's older form is من أين (min ayn) — real and respected, but وين is what you will hear from most people. Answer with من + place.
vocabulary.image_scene: A globe with a pin in Yemen and a second pin far away.

example.english: Where are you from? — From Sanaa

vocabulary.video_hint: The first question in any street interview.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Where do you live?' uses this rather than a verb: وين ساكن؟ Feminine ساكنة, plural ساكنين. The answer is ساكن في + place.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person standing at the door of a Sanaa house, keys in hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: 'Where do you live?' in interviews; house-tour openings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The answer to متزوج؟ when the answer is no. Feminine عزباء is formal; women more often say مش متزوجة. Also عزابي.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man alone at a café table with one glass of tea.
vocabulary.video_hint: Marriage talk in skits; 'still single' as the punchline.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Yemenis ask بلادك وين؟ — your 'country' meaning your home district or village, not your nation. Everyone is 'from' somewhere in the mountains even if born in Sanaa.
vocabulary.image_scene: Terraced green mountains with a stone village on the ridge.
vocabulary.video_hint: Villages and countryside vlogs; 'my bilaad' in the narration.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.arabic: أنا من أمريكا، بس ساكنة في صنعاء ذلحين.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min amriika, bass saakina fi ṣanʿaa dhalḥiin.
dialogue.english: I'm from America, but I live in Sanaa now.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.english: Of course not! I'm still studying.

dialogue.speaker: Um Ahmad
dialogue.english: Really? And how old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah
dialogue.arabic: يعني… ثنين وعشرين. وأنتي كم عمرش؟
dialogue.transliteration: yaʿni… thnayn w-ʿishriin. w-anti kam ʿumrish?
dialogue.english: Well… twenty-two. And how old are you?

sound_spotlight.explanation: One syllable with the ay diphthong, like English 'I' plus sh. Don't stretch it into two.
Addressing a woman, Sanaa turns the -ak ending into -ish. It is the most audible marker of the highland dialect; in Aden it stays -ik.
A yes/no question is the statement with the voice rising on the last syllable. Practise the same sentence as statement and question.

lesson_sequence.detail: Six short Q&A exchanges play as audio with pictures; the learner hears each question answered before any word is isolated.
ايش، مين، ليش، كيف، أي، كم on cards with audio and an example question each; English shown on the second pass.
Hear a question, tap the answer that fits (a place, a number, a person, a reason).
Um Ahmad asks the four small-talk questions; the learner picks or records an answer to each.
Given an answer, say the question. The app checks for the question word and the rise.
Counter rolls up; nudge to ask a real person three of these questions this week.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a Yemeni friend or your tutor three questions from this lesson — and answer theirs without hesitating over 'married?'.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on completion. Activates the small-talk set in both directions.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Listen for يعني in the next Yemeni video you watch and count how many times it appears in one minute.
real_world_prompts.context: Listening task; normalises the filler so the learner starts using it.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say إي instead of 'yes' for a whole day.

video_needs.scene: Street interviews and skits where a question is asked and answered on camera: where from, married, how many children, what work.
